newsitem.title: GERMANY: German father wins victory against spelling reform.
newsitem.headline: German father wins victory against spelling reform.

text.p: A planned reform of German spelling received a setback on Tuesday after a father of two schoolchildren won a court victory banning schools in the large central state of Hesse from teaching the new rules.

The controversial reform, which slashes the number of rules governing the language's notoriously tricky grammar, was agreed last year by Germany, Austria, Switzerland and other German-speaking communities.

But Hesse's state administrative court backed a petition by the father of two pupils in the town of Marburg that prevents the reform from being introduced in schools there as planned from August next year.

The court said in a statement that Germany's state culture ministers, who have spearheaded the changes despite widespread public indifference and some resistance, could not implement such a reform without formal law changes.
It added that there was also a risk that schoolchildren would be taught a way of writing that would be at odds with the way German was still written in wider society.

Opponents of the reform welcomed the ruling. "This completely unnecessary spelling reform has gained no democratic approval whatsoever," Hermann Otto Solms, parliamentary leader of the Free Democrats (FDP), told German radio.
Federal Education Minister Juergen Ruettgers said in a statement that it demonstrated that wider public and parliamentary discussion on the measures was needed.

The ruling of the Hesse court is open to appeal and has no bearing on that of other German states. One of them, Saxony-Anhalt, said it still planned to go ahead with the reform in the 1998/99 school-year.
